entries.content:
If you have certain lines of code that repeat over and over again in a project, there's a pretty standard solution for it: using a function.

But what about when you have the same project file setup that gets repeated over and over? How do you solve that?

Meet bash scripting. Bash scripts are written to execute certain sequences of commands on your machine automatically without you having to do anything. This is known as workflow automation, and that's what I'll be teaching you how to do in this article.

Table Of Contents

Prerequisites

To follow along with this article, you should have:

  • Git-bash installed on your machine
  • Some experience using a terminal or command prompt to run and execute commands (helpful but not required)
  • Understanding of basic programming concepts (like conditions and loops)
  • Docker installed on your machine
  • Basic understanding of Docker concepts (like images and containers)
  • Experience using Postgres (optional but recommended)

What Motivated This Project?

I was recently setting up a Docker image for Postgres on a few projects I was working on, and I noticed that I was following the same pattern in creating the images. The only difference was that they had different database credentials and database names.

I also realized that a large portion of today's rapidly developed apps tend to use Supabase as their backend, which can come with resource limits such as database storage, bandwidth, concurrent connections, and API request quotas (depending on the service tier and size of the project). And these issues can be solved by setting up your database.

So I thought, why not make a CLI tool that could automate creating Docker images for Postgres? That's when I learned about writing executable shell commands using bash to create workflow automations.

You can find the full working example used in this guide in this git-repo.

Introduction

Bash is a shell and scripting language used to write and execute commands or scripts that perform operations on a computer, such as creating directories and files, manipulating files, automating tasks, and managing system processes.

In this guide, you'll learn to automate the process of creating a Docker image for a Postgres database so that you don't have to create the image from scratch for each new project.

Bash Scripting File Setup

To get started, open you preferred text-editor and create a directory or folder there. Then within that directory, create a file with the extension 

.sh
.

At the beginning of a file, type:

#!/bin/bash


#!/bin/bash
(known as a "shebang") tells the operating system to run the script using the Bash shell, so the commands inside the file are executed as Bash/terminal commands.

Conditions in bash

After you've finished creating a script file and adding shebang, let's start by exploring how if statements are used in bash.

The syntax of 

if
looks like this:
if [[ condition ]];
    then
        command to execute
fi

The 

if
in bash is no different from what you're used to in other programming languages:
  • You use double square braces ([]) to add a condition you're checking against and a semicolon (;).
  • You use 
    then
    after the 
    if
    declaration to specify what should be executed if the condition is true.
  • You use the 
    fi
    to close the condition statement.

When you're writing the condition inside the square braces, make sure you leave a space before the condition and another one after it (as you can see in the code above). If you omit these spaces, you'll get errors.

Working Example:

Since we are automating Postgres database Docker image creation, first check if the file exists and has content. If it does have content, end the script. If not, we'll proceed with the next script.

#!/bin/bash

if [[ -s docker-compose.yml ]];
    then
        echo "The file already exists"
        exit 0
fi

echo "Next command"

In the if condition, we use the flag 

-s
to check if the file exists and has contents. File flags check file availability and permissions, and include but aren't limited to:
  • -f: used to check if the file exists
  • -s: used to check if the file exists and has contents
  • -d: used to check if a directory exists
  • -r: used to check if a file is readable
  • -w: used to check if a file is writable
  • -x: used to check if a file is executable

In the script, we're using 

-s
to check if a file named 
docker-compose.yml
exists in the directory where we're executing the command. If it's false, we use the 
echo
keyword to print the text "Next command". If it's true, we print the text "The file already exists".

exit
acts as a return keyword for bash scripting, 0 is used for success, and 1 is used for failure.

Let's test all this by creating a Docker Compose file and adding some content in the same directory where we're writing the bash script. In your terminal type 

bash name-of-file.sh
, and you should see "The file already exists":

But if we delete the content in the file and run the command again, we should see the output saying "Next command":

Interactive Shell

To make an automation dynamic and flexible you will need to receive inputs, take an example of a database name you won't always have the same database name, the name will change based on the project,

you do need to setup away to use a given name of the database when creating a new docker image for that you read inputs using the 

read
keyword.

There are different types of inputs based on the operation. And there are flags that are used to specify which type of input you're expecting, such as:

  • -p: for prompting the user to write a text
  • -s: used on passwords when you want the user input to stay hidden when writing it in the terminal
  • -a: used when you're expecting the user to pass in multiple inputs or if you're expecting an array from user.

Here's the syntax for reading user input:

read -p 'input_label: ' variable_name

Working Example:

Now let's create scripts to receive user input about the Postgres database image you're going to create.

#!/bin/bash

# database credentials
read -p 'DataBase-name(*): ' db
read -p 'DataBase-user(*): ' user
read -sp 'DataBase-password(*): ' pwd
echo
echo "your database is -> $db with a username of $user and a password of $pwd"

The script uses 

-p
on the 
read
keyword that prompts a string of text and 
-sp
that prompts the user to enter a string of text that's hidden (because the 
-s
hides what's being typed).

If you don't use the 

-p
option together with 
-s
, you won't be able to display a prompt asking the user to enter a password. With 
-s
alone, the input is hidden, but no prompt is shown unless you print one using 
echo
or 
printf
.

To print or use the input the user has added, use the dollar sign ($) followed with a variable name for the input you're expecting from the user. In the example above, we named the variable for getting the database name 

db
, so we'll use 
$db
when we want to access the name of the database the user has input.

Now if you run the script in the terminal, you should see a sequence of terminal prompts waiting for inputs. Once they're filled, you'll see all the input's values in the terminal:

How to Validate and Sanitize Input

You'll also need to validate input before executing anything. This is important because sometimes crucial field might be missing or mistyped. For example, you might forget to input the database name for the image you're trying to create.

When validating input, you'll use one of these flags (among others):

  • -z: checks if a variable value is empty
  • -n: checks if a variable value is not empty
  • -lt: checks if a number is less than a given number
  • -gt: checks if a number is greater than a given number
  • -eq: checks for equality of two values

You can use the 

-z
flag on every input that you need to make sure isn't empty before moving on to the next step:
#!/bin/bash

# database credentials
read -p 'DataBase-name(*): ' db
if [[ -z $db ]]
    then
        echo "The database field cannot be empty!"
        exit 1
fi

read -p 'DataBase-user(*): ' user
if [[ -z $user ]]
    then
        echo "The user field cannot be empty!"
        exit 1
fi

read -sp 'DataBase-password(*): ' pwd
if [[ -z $pwd ]]
    then
        echo "The password field cannot be empty!"
        exit 1
fi

This script helps you make sure that all critical information about the database is present before proceeding to another input.

Default Values

You may want some fields to use default value (for example, the container name of the image, port, or volume of the container). For such scenarios you can use 

:=
to assign a variable default value:
#!/bin/bash

# container information
read -p 'Container-name: ' container_name
read -p 'Container-port(if omitted, the container will use default postgresql default port of 5432): ' port
read -p 'Volume-name: ' vol_name

echo "container-name-> ${container_name:=cont_one}, port->${port:=5432}, volume_name->${vol_name:=backend_data}"

When you run the script and skip all three of those inputs, bash will use the default value(s) you've used as fallbacks.

But if you pass value for those inputs, bash uses the provided values. For example, supply all three inputs and see the output you get:

How to Create and Write to a File

Now that you know how to create a Docker image for a Postgres database, you need to create a 

docker-compose.yml
file that will be executed when starting and stopping your containers.

In Bash, there are multiple ways of creating a file:

  • First, you can use 
    > filename
    . This creates a file if it doesn't exist. If it exists, its contents are overwritten (replaced).
  • There's also 
    >> filename
    : This appends contents to a file or creates a file if one doesn't exist.
  • Finally, there's 
    touch filename
    : This creates a file if it doesn't exist. If the file already exists, its contents are preserved and only the file's timestamps are updated.

How to Use 
>
to Create and Write to a File

When you want to create a file and write content to it at the same time, you'll want to use echo in front of 

>
and then add the filename, like this:
#!/bin/bash

echo Hello> test.txt

This will create a 

test.txt
file with "hello" as content inside.

How to Use 
>>
to Append Contents to an Existing File

To append contents to an existing file, add the contents before the 

>>
and then follow with the filename you want to append content onto. Let's add Africa after Hello in the 
test.txt
file we created in the previous script.
#!/bin/bash

echo Africa!>> test.txt

Now test.txt will have Hello and Africa! on the new line.

Using those symbols, let's create a 

docker-compose.yml
file that will hold contents about our Postgres database setup.
#!/bin/bash

> docker-compose.yml

And just like that you have your docker-compose file created in your directory.

How to Write Multiple Different Contents to a File

You can also use the 

cat
keyword to write to a file. Typically, 
cat
is used for reading the contents of a file. But when you combine it with 
< and the sign for appending contents to a file 
>>
 (that we just discussed), you can add multiple contents to a file in the format you want. The syntax looks like this:
# writing docker compose contents

cat <> docker-compose.yml

  # file contents
EOF



The 
< tells bash to write contents to a file until it finds the EOF keyword (end of file). Then you use 
>> filename
 to append the contents to the file. With a Docker compose setup it would look like this:
#!/bin/bash

#file creation and writing
 >  docker-compose.yml

cat<>docker-compose.yml
 services:
    postgres:
        image: postgres:18-alpine
        container_name: ${container_name:= $db}

        environment:
            POSTGRES_USER: $user
            POSTGRES_PASSWORD: $pwd
            POSTGRES_database: $db

        ports:
            - ${port:=5432}:5432
        volumes:
            - ${vol_name:=database-data}:/var/postgresql

 volumes:
    ${vol_name:=database-data}:

EOF



Bash Arguments and Flags
With Bash arguments, you can pass values in the same line while executing a script. To use arguments, add the values while executing the script on the same line, like this:
bash script val1 val2 



To read arguments value(s), use the dollar sign ($) followed by the position in which you inputted your values (positions start at 1, not 0).
In the example, if you want to echo the content of the second argument value, you can use 
echo $2
.
To understand this better, let's enhance data input experience by passing the database credentials on the fly using arguments:
#!/bin/bash

# database credentials

if [[ -z $1 ]]; then
    read -p 'DataBase-name(*): ' db
 else
    db="$1"
fi

# database checking and validating

if [[ -z $2 ]]; then
    read -p 'DataBase-user(*): ' user
 else
    user="$2"
fi

# user checking and validating

if [[ -z $1 ]]; then
    read -sp 'DataBase-password(*): ' pwd
 else
    pwd=$3
fi

# password vaidation and checking



The snippet first checks if there's an argument. If there aren't any, you use the prompt to input the value. If there are arguments, you assign the argument value to a variable that represents the given database credentials (database name, password, and so on...). Now you can run the script with arguments:
bash image.sh customers ABC-Company secret123!



The image that will be created from the above script will have a database of 
customers
, user 
ABC-Company
, and a password of 
secret123!
.
Bash Flags/Options
The script has a section that asks for information about the image that you're creating, but the info can be optional. With bash option/flags, you can skip the step that prompts for container information input using the 
-D
 option. This lets you explicitly keep the default container info before the script runs.
Here's an example:
#!/bin/bash

while getopts "ny" options; do
	case "$options" in
		n) echo "You choose no";;
		y) echo "You choose yes";;
		*) echo "No such option/flag"; exit 1;;
    esac
done

shift $((OPTIND - 1))



In the above script:
  • The while loop keeps running as long as 
    getopts
     isn't empty
  • getopts
     gets the passed option in the script
  • "ny"
     are the options we're expecting from user when running the script
  • options
     is a variable that will keep track of the input option between "n" and "y"
  • do
     starts the loop
  • case
     checks if the selected option is in the defined option using the 
    in
     keyword
  • We then define what happens when we call the script with the option 
    -n
     or 
    -y
     and use a double semi-colon (;;) to close the option definition
  • The 
    *
     is used in case the input options aren't defined.
  • esac
     then closes the case
  • done
     ends the loop so the loop doesn't continue running forever
  • shift $((OPTIND - 1))
     helps avoid a conflict that may occur when the script also expects arguments by shifting the remaining arguments left over the flags, effectively discarding the flags from the parameter list.
You can then apply the syntax in the script to skip the step that asks for container info when 
-D
 is passed as an option during the script execution.
#!/bin/bash

ask_container_info=true

while getopts "D" options; do
	case "$options" in
		D) ask_container_info=false;;
		*) echo "No such option/flag"; exit 1;;
    esac
done

shift $((OPTIND - 1))

if [[ $ask_container_info == true ]]; then
	#Prompt the user to input custom container information
    read -p 'Container-name: ' container_name
    read -p 'Container-port(if omitted, the container will use default postgresql default port of 5432): ' port
    read -p 'Volume-name: ' vol_name
fi



There is one option here, which is why the option section only has 
D
. 
ask_container_info
 starts as true, meaning unless the option is passed, the script will prompt the user to enter the container information. We then change the value of 
ask_container_info
 to false when the 
-D
 is passed with the script's execution.
How to Make Your Scripts Executable and Available on Your PC's Path
The next step is to make the script available and executable in every terminal you use on your machine. At the moment, the script just works in the current directory you're using to create and write your scripts.
We'll start by making the script file executable and remove the file extension from the file, so we don't need to always call our script with the 
.sh
 extension.
How to Make a File Executable
To make a file executable, use the Linux 
chmod
 command. It stands for change mode. Mode includes file permissions like write, read, and execute.
chmod +x image



Here, 
x
 makes the file executable, and then you've listed the file name you want to make executable (
image
).
How to Add Your Directory to the 
system/machine
 Path


To make this available in every terminal you open, regardless of the directory, you'll need to register your scripts in the system paths where all global scripts and commands are stored.
To do that, copy the full path of your directory and then in your terminal type the following:
export PATH="$PATH:"



Replace 
 with your directory. This command will add the script directory into the current working terminal. But if you try to switch to another terminal and run your script, it'll fail.
Now let's configure the directory globally so every terminal will be able to execute the script:
nano ~/.bash_profile



After this you should see something that looks like this:
You can see in the image above that I already have my path declared in the file (see the selected text).
If it's not in you're file, you can copy-paste 
export PATH="$PATH:"
 inside the file. When you're done, press 
Ctrl+O
 and then 
enter
 to save. Then press 
Ctrl+x
 to exit the nano editor.
Then re-load the machine path again to include your scripts there:
source ~/.bash_profile



After this, you'll be able to run your script in any terminal on your machine using the script file name only (I named my file 
image
):
Conclusion
In this guide, you learned how to create your own scripts to automate your workflows. I hope it helps you reduce the amount of energy and time you waste on repetitive tasks that can be automated using script commands.
You can find the full working CLI tool that we used as an example in this guide on this git-repo. There you'll find the installation guide and usage tips. If you find it helpful, please consider starring the repo and sharing it with your collogues who might benefit from it.
Thanks!

entries.title: How to Partner with Design Studios on Client Builds: A Freelance Developer's Guide
entries.summary: Let's say a design studio gets a new client project. The branding is ready, the wireframes are approved, the Figma file is polished, and every screen looks pretty much perfect. Then the developer join
entries.content:
Let's say a design studio gets a new client project. The branding is ready, the wireframes are approved, the Figma file is polished, and every screen looks pretty much perfect. Then the developer joins the project. You say, “Here are the designs. Can you build this?”

That sounds simple, until the first question appears. What happens when the mobile version doesn't exist? What if the animation that looks perfect in Figma performs badly on a real phone? Who decides what happens when the client requests Google login three days before launch? And when a technical problem appears, does the developer speak directly to the client or go through the studio?

These questions aren't unimportant side issues. They're part of building the product. Research on designer-developer collaboration supports this. A 2025 systematic review covering 45 papers found recurring challenges around how designers and developers communicate, coordinate work, and understand each other's responsibilities.

If you're a freelance developer, your job isn't just about writing code. You also need to make sure that design, technology, scope, communication and client expectations are moving in the same direction.

In this guide, we'll look at how you can work effectively with design studios, from understanding project requirements and handling design handoffs to managing client expectations and technical challenges. We'll also cover some practical ways to make sure projects move smoothly from the initial design to the final launch.

What We'll Cover Here:

First, Understand What the Design Studio Is Actually Hiring You For

This is an important section because freelancers often misunderstand their exact role in a project. A design studio or a branding agency might hire you for frontend development, full-stack development, prototyping, or straight design to code implementation. They might also bring you in for CMS integration, API integration, performance optimization, or ongoing maintenance after launch.

But the role can vary dramatically depending on the studio's internal capabilities and the client's specific needs.

Are You the Developer, the Technical Partner, or Just the Implementer?

You must explain the difference and define your boundaries.

As an implementer, you simply receive finished designs and build them exactly as specified without questioning the logic. As a developer, you build the product but also actively raise technical concerns when you spot potential issues. As a technical partner, you get involved much earlier in the process and help determine what can actually be built within the budget and timeline.

Clarifying this exact dynamic before starting the work prevents many structural problems later.

Don't Start Coding Until You Understand the Project

A Figma file can tell you exactly what something looks like on a screen. It doesn't necessarily tell you how it should behave in the real world.

It won't show you what happens when data is missing from the server. It doesn't explain what happens on slow cellular networks or what happens on obscure mobile devices. It also leaves out what happens when user-generated text becomes too long or when users make critical mistakes. And it doesn't talk about which interactions are absolutely essential, and which parts are merely visual prototypes rather than final requirements.

Ask Questions Before Opening Your Code Editor

You need a practical checklist to run through before touching your keyboard.

Regarding the product, ask: What problem is the product solving? Who is using it? What's the single most important user action?

Regarding the design, ask: Are these designs entirely final? Are there dedicated mobile and tablet versions available? Are all the shown animations part of the strict requirement?

Regarding the technical side, ask: Is there an existing backend in place? What specific technology stack is expected? Are all necessary APIs already available? Who handles the hosting environment?

Regarding the client, ask: Who communicates directly with the client? Who ultimately approves changes? Who gives you final feedback?

Google's engineering guidance similarly stresses clear objectives and requirements because poor communication and vague expectations directly contribute to project failures

Treat the Figma File as a Conversation, Not a Contract

Explain to your partners that developers shouldn't treat design files as sacred objects that must be reproduced pixel for pixel regardless of technical reality. Instead, treat them as a starting point for an ongoing discussion.

For example, a designer creates a complex scrolling animation that looks genuinely great in the initial prototype. But during implementation you discover that it causes massive performance issues on lower-end mobile devices.

The wrong approach is saying something like: "The design says so, so I'll build it anyway." Another wrong approach is shutting it down by saying: "That simply won't work."

A much better approach is saying something along the lines of: "This interaction is entirely possible, but it may affect performance on mobile devices. Could we simplify the animation specifically for smaller screens?" That's constructive technical feedback without turning the conversation into a hostile design vs development argument.

This dynamic is supported by a comprehensive 2025 systematic review of designer-developer collaboration, which revealed that separate decision-making procedures and a lack of mutual understanding are persistent challenges in the field.

Define Who Owns Which Decisions

This is especially important when you're a freelancer working directly between a studio and its end client. You need to create a simple, clear responsibility framework. Usually, visual design is led solely by the design studio. UX decisions are generally handled by the design studio alongside the client.

Technical architecture, database structure and API implementation are led exclusively by the developer. Product priorities are decided by the client and the studio. Technical feasibility falls entirely to the developer. Final design approval rests with the client and the studio.

Emphasize that this framework isn't totally rigid. The important thing is universally knowing who has the final say in any given category.

The One Question Every Freelancer Should Ask

"If we disagree about a design or technical decision, who makes the final call?" That one specific question can save countless hours of confusion and resentment later in the process.

Set Up a Workflow That Doesn't Depend on Constant Messages

A simple, predictable workflow eliminates chaos, and you can systematically organize a standard workflow.

First is the brief, followed by the design review. Next comes technical planning and then the actual development phase. After that is the internal review, followed by client feedback. This leads to the revision stage, moving into QA and finally culminating in the launch.

Explaining each phase briefly ensures everyone knows where the project stands at any given moment.

Give Every Stage a Clear "Done"

For example, a design review is officially complete when desktop and mobile designs exist, missing interactive states are identified, visual assets are available, and complex interactions are understood.

The development phase is complete when the feature actually works, responsive behavior is thoroughly checked, known bugs are actively documented, and the studio has a functional review build.

This clarity inherently prevents the classic miscommunication of: "I thought you were still working on it."

Create a Single Source of Truth

The core problem with freelance collaborations is that crucial information can become quickly scattered across Slack, email, WhatsApp, Figma comments, GitHub, Notion, Google Docs, random video calls, and text messages. Then six days later someone inevitably asks: "Why did we decide to remove that specific feature?" Nobody likely remembers the exact reason.

Recommend having one centralized place for core requirements, open questions, finalized decisions, technical constraints, scope changes, project deadlines and feedback.

An observational study of software developers' work practices found that developers spend about 45% of their time collaborating with colleagues and seeking information, making information visibility an essential part of software work. Google's SRE guidance also recommends writing decisions and project information down to heavily reduce problems caused by distance and fragmented communication.

Handle Design Handoffs Like an Engineer

Instead of simply receiving a Figma link and guessing what to do, create a proper, methodical handoff checklist. Check typography, colors, spacing and breakpoints. Verify all assets, icons, component states and hover states. Confirm loading states, error states and empty states. Double-check mobile behavior, accessibility requirements and complex animations.

Look for the Screens That Don't Exist

Designers naturally often show the happy path where everything works perfectly. But developers absolutely have to build the empty dashboards and the failed API requests. You must account for loading screens, invalid forms, expired sessions, and missing images. You have to handle long usernames breaking the layout and slow connections timing out. This is precisely where developers add tangible value beyond simply translating a Figma canvas into HTML, CSS, and JavaScript.

Scope Creep Is Easier to Prevent Than to Fight

The studio might initially say: "The client also wants a small dashboard." Then a few days later: "Can we subtly add notifications?" Then the next week: "Could we also seamlessly add Google login?"

None of these requests sound huge individually. But together, they can easily turn a straightforward two week project into an exhausting month-long project.

Use a Simple Change Rule

Whenever something new appears in the pipeline, ask a series of questions. Is this part of the original scope? How much active work will it require? Does it negatively affect the deadline? Does it conflict with another feature? Who formally approves the change?

Don't make the section sound like aggressive negotiation advice. Frame it entirely as protecting the overall project from unclear expectations and budget overruns.

Don't Hide Technical Problems Until the Deadline

Explain the freelancer's ethical and professional responsibility here. If you discover the API isn't actually ready, state it immediately. If the animation isn't practical, the design doesn't account for accessibility, the database structure needs completely changing, or a feature will take three days instead of three hours, say it early. Not two agonizing days before the scheduled launch. You can introduce a very simple principle: bad news gets significantly more expensive when you delay it.

Review the Build Together, Not Just at the End

Explain clearly why continuous reviews are infinitely better than one giant final review at the very end of the timeline. A suggested review rhythm keeps everyone in the loop.

After a major component is finished, conduct a studio review. After the main page is completed, run a design review. After responsive implementation is coded, initiate a mobile review. Before the actual launch, perform a full QA.

This creates significantly smaller, highly manageable feedback loops. Instead of hearing: "The entire website is completely wrong," you get: "The spacing on this specific card is 4px too large." This is much easier and cheaper to fix.

Learn to Push Back Without Becoming Difficult to Work With

Developers sometimes respond to highly unrealistic requirements with a flat: "That's impossible."

Instead, you should frame it differently: "We can certainly build this, but there are two distinct trade-offs." Then explain the available paths clearly. Option A is visually closer to the design, but requires much more development time. Option B is a much simpler implementation, delivering significantly better performance. Option C is to keep the current approach for desktop interfaces and drastically simplify it on mobile devices.

This directly makes the developer a strategic problem solver rather than someone who simply says yes or no to every request.

Keep the Relationship Healthy After Launch

The professional relationship shouldn't abruptly end the exact second the site goes live on the server. Clarify the boundaries of the bug-fix period and ongoing maintenance. Discuss future features, hosting responsibilities and comprehensive documentation. Manage the handover of access credentials and establish clear code ownership.

Most importantly, don't ever leave ownership ambiguous. The design studio should confidently know what happens if the client comes back three months later aggressively asking for a brand new feature.

A Simple Collaboration Checklist for Freelance Developers

Before the project officially starts, thoroughly define the core business logic, clarify your exact engineering responsibilities, and audit the UI/UX designs for edge cases or missing interactive states.

Once you understand the primary goals, confirm the complete technology stack, from the frontend framework to the database architecture, while setting strict boundaries around API dependencies, version control repositories, and sprint deadlines.

As you move into active development, consistently flag performance bottlenecks or query inefficiencies early, ensuring you document all major architectural shifts within your codebase. Rather than jumping straight into writing, break down the visual files into reusable component logic and shared design tokens before implementation begins. You should also share live staging builds frequently, track scope creep meticulously through an issue tracker, and continuously test how your DOM renders across various viewport breakpoints to catch responsive errors.

Finally, before pushing to the production environment, audit the compiled build against the original designs to ensure high-fidelity accuracy. Rigorously test state management across critical user routing flows, debug any layout shifts on mobile browsers, and verify that your semantic HTML meets baseline WCAG accessibility standards.

To wrap up the collaboration seamlessly, lock down the CI/CD deployment pipeline responsibilities and hand over a comprehensively documented repository that clearly explains the environmental variables, build scripts, and third-party integrations the studio will need moving forward.

Final Thoughts

A Figma file shows how a product should look, while development reveals everything it needs to handle when real people start using it.

That's why working with a design studio involves more than a simple design-to-code handoff. You'll also need to catch technical problems early, keep responsibilities clear, and make decisions before small issues become launch-day problems.

Throughout the project, stay in touch with the design team, share your technical concerns, and discuss changes before they affect the timeline. This will make it easier to handle unexpected problems and deliver a product that works well for the client and the people who will eventually use it.
