entries.summary: A vector database stores data as lists of numbers called embeddings, which lets it search by meaning instead of matching exact keywords. It's the piece behind a lot of recommendation systems, RAG apps
entries.content:
A vector database stores data as lists of numbers called embeddings, which lets it search by meaning instead of matching exact keywords. It's the piece behind a lot of recommendation systems, RAG apps, and AI agents.

We just published a comprehensive course on the freeCodeCamp.org YouTube channel that will teach you how vector databases work, starting with the math and ending with a working semantic search project. This course is from codeEdx, whose instructor has worked as a software engineer for 15 years and as a lead AI engineer for the last four. No prior knowledge is required.

In this course, you will learn:

  • Vectors & Similarity Math

    Learn what a vector is and how cosine similarity and Euclidean distance measure how close two pieces of data are.
  • Tokens & Tokenization

    See why AI models can't read raw text and how a tokenizer splits a word like "indivisible" into more than one token.
  • Embeddings & Embedding Models

    Understand how text becomes vectors that capture meaning, including the classic king minus man plus woman equals queen example.
  • Generating Embeddings with Gemini

    Follow a live demo using Google's Gemini embedding model, then visualize the results in 3D with principal component analysis (PCA).
  • Inside a Vector Database

    Explore the storage, indexing, and query processing layers, and how IVF and HNSW indexes avoid slow brute force search.
  • Semantic Search with ChromaDB

    Create a Chroma client and collection, store your embeddings, and run queries that return results based on meaning.

Watch the full course on the freeCodeCamp.org YouTube channel (1.5-hour watch).

entries.title: How to Detect Financial Fraud Patterns with Knowledge Graphs: A Production Guide
entries.summary: Most anti-fraud architectures in enterprise payment workflows evaluate transactions in isolation. When an invoice arrives, an automated rules engine checks it against static thresholds. It checks whet
entries.content:
Most anti-fraud architectures in enterprise payment workflows evaluate transactions in isolation.

When an invoice arrives, an automated rules engine checks it against static thresholds. It checks whether the dollar amount falls within normal limits, whether the vendor is on an approved vendor list, and whether the submitting IP address looks familiar. If the individual attributes look plausible, the payment clears.

The problem with this approach is structural. Sophisticated fraud schemes like money mule rings, circular invoicing loops, and vendor collision rarely produce transactions that alert individual thresholds. A shell company invoicing $4,800 to stay under a $5,000 dual sign-off threshold looks completely fine in isolation. But when 25 seemingly independent vendors all route disbursements to the same bank account, the coordinated pattern starts to become clear.

You won't find the warning in the attributes of an isolated transaction. It lives in the topology of the payment network.

In a relational database, tracing these multi-entity relationships requires recursive cell joins across tables of vendors, invoices, payments, and bank accounts. But as tables grow into millions of rows, deep path traversals quickly degrade query performance. Graph databases solve this by storing relationships as first-class, index-free adjacency pointers, turning multi-hop traversals into constant-time lookups.

In this tutorial, you'll explore the architecture of an end-to-end relational fraud detection pipeline built on Neo4j. You'll see how to model financial entities as a graph, precompute derived edges to optimize query latency, and write parameterized Cypher queries to uncover five core procurement fraud schemes.

The complete reference implementation is available in the fraud-detection-knowledge-graphs repository.

What We'll Cover:

Why Tabular Rules Miss Relational Fraud

In accounts payable pipelines, risk checks typically operate on isolated records:

# Transaction-level view — nothing suspicious
transactions = [
    {"vendor": "Alpha Corp", "amount": 5200.00, "date": "2025-08-01"},
    {"vendor": "Beta LLC", "amount": 4800.00, "date": "2025-08-02"},
    {"vendor": "Gamma Inc", "amount": 5100.00, "date": "2025-08-03"},
]
# All amounts within normal range ($1K–$15K). All vendors valid.
# Dates are sequential. Nothing triggers any rule.

When you map those same records to an interconnected graph, the hidden structure becomes clear right away:

# Graph view — all three vendors pay to the same account
connections = {
    "ACC-MULE-001": ["Alpha Corp", "Beta LLC", "Gamma Inc"],
    "ACC-0042":     ["Delta Corp", "Epsilon LLC"],
    "ACC-0099":     ["Zeta GmbH"],
}
# ACC-MULE-001 receives from 25+ vendors. That's a money mule ring.
# The convergence is the red flag.

The underlying data hasn't changed. But when you evaluate transactions within an entity graph, the coordinated funnel stands out.

In a relational database, connecting these dots requires multiple joins across separate table. In a knowledge graph, the connections are stored directly as edges connecting nodes, which allows you to query them in a single traversal.

PatternWhat It IsWhat Traditional Tools Don't Catch
Duplicate InvoicesSame invoice and vendor, near-identical amount, close datesExact match misses slight variations
Circular RingsVendors invoicing each other in a closed loopEach invoice looks legitimate alone
Money Mule RingsMany vendors funneling to one controlled accountNo single payment is anomalous
Vendor CollusionIndependent-looking vendors sharing underlying attributesNo cluster detection across entities
Payment AnomaliesInvoice approved by someone outside their department's authorityRole-based checks pass, context checks don't exist

A knowledge graph doesn't replace rules engines or ML models. But it does fill the gap they can't reach: relationships.

Prerequisites

To follow along with this tutorial, you'll need:

  • Python 3.10 or higher installed on your machine.
  • Docker and Docker Compose installed to run a local Neo4j instance.
  • Basic familiarity with Python and database concepts.

How to Model the Financial Graph and Ingestion Schema

Before running fraud queries, you need to structure your data into a cohesive property graph. The reference dataset models six entity types commonly found in financial systems:

EntityKey PropertiesRole
Vendortax_id, name, country, cityWho issues invoices
Invoiceinvoice_id, amount, date, categoryWhat was billed
Paymentpayment_id, amount, dateWhat was paid
BankAccountaccount_id, routing_number, bank_nameWhere money went
Employeeemployee_id, name, departmentWho approved
Organizationorg_id, name, departmentsStructural hierarchy

The base relationships form a bipartite payment network:

(Employee)-[:APPROVED]->(Payment)-[:LINKED_TO]->(Invoice)-[:ISSUED_BY]->(Vendor)
                                   |
                                   v
                            (Payment)-[:PAID_TO]->(BankAccount)

Step 1: How to Generate the Dataset with Known Injected Patterns

Real-world financial datasets are difficult to access because of privacy and regulatory restrictions. Using synthetic data allows you to inject known fraud patterns and systematically verify that your detection queries find them.

The dataset generator creates approximately 500 entities with five known patterns embedded:

  • 12 duplicate invoice pairs
  • 1 circular invoice ring (3 vendors)
  • 1 money mule ring (25 vendors for 1 account)
  • 1 vendor collusion cluster (4 vendors)
  • 3 payment anomalies
from dataset.generate import FraudDatasetGenerator

gen = FraudDatasetGenerator(
    num_vendors=100,
    num_employees=30,
    num_organizations=5,
    seed=42,
)
output_dir = gen.save("dataset/output")

Setting a fixed 

seed=42
makes the dataset fully reproducible. Running the generator produces the exact same fraud patterns each time, giving you a reliable benchmark for testing queries:
Vendors: 100
Invoices: 220 (200 base + 20 fraud)
Payments: 331 (300 base + 31 fraud)
Bank Accounts: 51 (50 + 1 mule)
Employees: 30
Organizations: 5
Fraud Patterns: 5 types

The generator also exports a ground-truth manifest 

ground_truth.json
that logs every injected anomaly, and this serves as your automated validation oracle.

Step 2: How to Connect to Neo4j and Create Constraints

You can spin up a local Neo4j 5.20 container with APOC procedures enabled using Docker Compose:

docker compose up -d

Next, initialize the database driver and establish uniqueness constraints:

from graph.connection import FraudGraph

with FraudGraph() as graph:
    graph.create_constraints()

These constraints are critical for query performance. In Neo4j, unique property constraints automatically build underlying B-tree indexes. Without them, every MERGE operation forces an unindexed full scan across all nodes in the database:

class FraudGraph:
    def __init__(self, uri=None, user=None, password=None):
        self.uri = uri or os.environ.get('NEO4J_URI', 'bolt://localhost:7687')
        self.user = user or os.environ.get('NEO4J_USER', 'neo4j')
        self.password = password or os.environ.get('NEO4J_PASSWORD', 'password')
        self.driver = None

    def connect(self):
        self.driver = GraphDatabase.driver(
            self.uri, auth=(self.user, self.password),
            max_connection_pool_size=50,
            connection_acquisition_timeout=30,
        )
        with self.driver.session() as session:
            session.run('RETURN 1')
        return self

    def __enter__(self):
        self.connect()
        return self

    def __exit__(self, exc_type, exc_val, exc_tb):
        self.close()

    def create_constraints(self):
        with self.driver.session() as session:
            session.run("CREATE CONSTRAINT vendor_tax_id IF NOT EXISTS FOR (v:Vendor) REQUIRE v.tax_id IS UNIQUE")
            session.run("CREATE CONSTRAINT invoice_id IF NOT EXISTS FOR (i:Invoice) REQUIRE i.invoice_id IS UNIQUE")
            session.run("CREATE CONSTRAINT account_id IF NOT EXISTS FOR (a:BankAccount) REQUIRE a.account_id IS UNIQUE")
            session.run("CREATE CONSTRAINT employee_id IF NOT EXISTS FOR (e:Employee) REQUIRE e.employee_id IS UNIQUE")

Step 3: How to Load Entities into the Graph

The 

FraudGraphLoader
uses Cypher's 
UNWIND
to batch-insert entities in parameterized transactions:
from graph.loader import FraudGraphLoader

with FraudGraph() as graph:
    graph.create_constraints()
    loader = FraudGraphLoader(graph)
    loader.load_all(data)

The loading sequence respects foreign key dependencies: organizations are loaded first, followed by vendors, bank accounts, and employees, with invoices and payments loaded last.

Each load method follows the same pattern:

UNWIND $data AS v
MERGE (vendor:Vendor {tax_id: v.tax_id})
SET vendor.name = v.name,
    vendor.country = v.country,
    vendor.city = v.city
WITH vendor, v
MATCH (org:Organization {org_id: v.organization})
MERGE (vendor)-[:BELONGS_TO]->(org)


MERGE
creates or matches a node (using the constraint for O(1) lookup), 
SET
attaches properties, and 
MERGE
on the relationship connects nodes.

Step 4: How to Materialize Derived Relationships for Fast Queries

A central architectural decision in graph databases is deciding whether to compute relationships at query time or materialize them during ingestion.

Discovering whether two vendors share a bank account requires traversing a four-hop path:

(Vendor)<-[:ISSUED_BY]-(Invoice)<-[:LINKED_TO]-(Payment)-[:PAID_TO]->(BankAccount)<-[:PAID_TO]-(Payment)-[:LINKED_TO]->(Invoice)-[:ISSUED_BY]->(Vendor)

Evaluating this four-hop path during every real-time fraud query causes significant computational overhead. Instead, you can materialize derived edges when data enters the system. This adds a slight write latency during batch ingestion, but it turns multi-hop traversals into direct, single-hop lookups during runtime detection queries.

The first derived relationship is SHARED_ACCOUNT_WITH, which links vendors that share a destination bank account:

MATCH (v1:Vendor)<-[:ISSUED_BY]-(i1:Invoice)<-[:LINKED_TO]-(p1:Payment)-[:PAID_TO]->(a:BankAccount)
MATCH (v2:Vendor)<-[:ISSUED_BY]-(i2:Invoice)<-[:LINKED_TO]-(p2:Payment)-[:PAID_TO]->(a)
WHERE id(v1) < id(v2)
MERGE (v1)-[:SHARED_ACCOUNT_WITH]->(v2)

The filter 

WHERE id(v1) < id(v2)
ensures that the relationship is stored as a single directed edge between the internal node IDs, which prevents duplicate reverse edges.

You can also materialize shared geographic locations and banking routing prefixes to detect loose collusion networks:

-- Same city and country
MATCH (v1:Vendor), (v2:Vendor)
WHERE id(v1) < id(v2)
  AND v1.city = v2.city
  AND v1.country = v2.country
MERGE (v1)-[:SHARED_LOCATION]->(v2)

-- Bank accounts with same routing prefix (first 3 digits)
MATCH (v1:Vendor)<-[:ISSUED_BY]-(i1:Invoice)<-[:LINKED_TO]-(p1:Payment)-[:PAID_TO]->(a1:BankAccount)
MATCH (v2:Vendor)<-[:ISSUED_BY]-(i2:Invoice)<-[:LINKED_TO]-(p2:Payment)-[:PAID_TO]->(a2:BankAccount)
WHERE id(v1) < id(v2)
  AND a1.account_id <> a2.account_id
  AND substring(a1.routing_number, 0, 3) = substring(a2.routing_number, 0, 3)
MERGE (v1)-[:SHARED_ROUTING_PREFIX]->(v2)

Once ingestion completes, you can inspect the graph topology to confirm that both base and derived relationships loaded properly:

info = graph.get_info()
for label, count in sorted(info['nodes'].items(), key=lambda x: -x[1]):
    print(f"  {label}: {count} nodes")
for rel, count in sorted(info['relationships'].items(), key=lambda x: -x[1]):
    print(f"  {rel}: {count} relationships")

The output shows raw entities and the generated derived relationships:

  Invoice: 220 nodes
  Payment: 331 nodes
  Vendor: 100 nodes
  BankAccount: 51 nodes
  Employee: 30 nodes

  SHARED_ACCOUNT_WITH: 412 relationships
  SHARED_LOCATION: 387 relationships
  LINKED_TO: 331 relationships
  PAID_TO: 331 relationships
  ISSUED_BY: 220 relationships
  APPROVED: 331 relationships
  SHARED_ROUTING_PREFIX: 52 relationships

These derived relationships are designed specifically for high-speed detection. In a relational database, discovering shared accounts requires a self-join across multiple tables. In a graph, it becomes a precomputed edge, turning complex traversals into direct lookups.

How to Detect Five Fraud Patterns with Cypher Queries

Once your schema and derived relationships are established, you can construct parameterized Cypher queries that'll flag five widespread procurement fraud patterns.

Pattern 1: How to Find Duplicate Invoices

Fraudulent actors often submit duplicate invoices spaced days or weeks apart, assuming accounts payable teams will process them as routine recurring expenses.

Rule-based engines often catch exact matches, but they can miss invoices with slight date shifts. In a graph, you can query across all invoices issued by the same vendor within a rolling date window:

// graph/queries.py — detect_duplicates()
MATCH (v:Vendor)<-[:ISSUED_BY]-(i1:Invoice),
      (v)<-[:ISSUED_BY]-(i2:Invoice)
WHERE i1.invoice_id < i2.invoice_id
  AND i1.amount = i2.amount
  AND i1.date < i2.date
  AND duration.between(date(i1.date), date(i2.date)).days <= $max_days
RETURN i1.invoice_id AS invoice_a,
       i2.invoice_id AS invoice_b,
       v.name AS vendor,
       i1.amount AS amount,
       i1.date AS date_a,
       i2.date AS date_b,
       duration.between(date(i1.date), date(i2.date)).days AS days_apart
ORDER BY days_apart

Key points here:

  • The condition 
    i1.invoice_id < i2.invoice_id
    prevents returning the same pair twice like 
    (A, B)
    and 
    (B, A)
    .
  • i1.amount = i2.amount
    is the fraud signal: same amount means likely the same invoice submitted twice.
  • By scoping the search to invoices issued by the same vendor v, the query leverages index lookups on the vendor before evaluating date intervals with the native temporal duration.between() function.

You can execute this query through the Python wrapper:

from graph.queries import FraudQueries

queries = FraudQueries(graph)
duplicates = queries.detect_duplicates(max_days_apart=14)
print(f"Found {len(duplicates)} duplicate invoice pairs")
for dup in duplicates[:5]:
    print(f"  {dup['invoice_a']} ↔ {dup['invoice_b']} | "
          f"{dup['vendor']} | ${dup['amount']} | "
          f"{dup['days_apart']} days apart")

The query detects all 12 duplicate pairs injected into the synthetic dataset, achieving 100% recall.

Pattern 2: How to Uncover Circular Invoicing Rings

In circular invoicing schemes, three or more vendors bill one another in a closed loop. Each transaction appears legitimate on its own, but no actual goods or services are delivered.

Because you precomputed 

SHARED_ACCOUNT_WITH
, cycle detection is simplified to finding three-node triangles in the vendor sub-graph:
// graph/queries.py — detect_circular_schemes()
MATCH path = (v1:Vendor)-[:SHARED_ACCOUNT_WITH]-(v2:Vendor)
              -[:SHARED_ACCOUNT_WITH]-(v3:Vendor)
              -[:SHARED_ACCOUNT_WITH]-(v1)
WHERE id(v1) < id(v2) AND id(v2) < id(v3)
RETURN path,
       [n IN nodes(path) | {name: n.name, tax_id: n.tax_id}] AS vendors,
       length(path) AS hops

Key points here:

  • The constraint 
    id(v1) < id(v2)
    AND 
    id(v2) < id(v3)
    eliminates cyclic permutations. Without it, a single three-node ring 
    (A, B, C)
    would be returned three separate times.
  • If you ran this query directly over raw four-hop transactional paths without materialized edges, finding a three-cycle would require traversing twelve hops, which causes high CPU usage on large datasets.
circles = queries.detect_circular_schemes(min_cycle_length=3)
print(f"Found {len(circles)} circular invoice rings")
for ring in circles:
    vendor_names = [v['name'] for v in ring['vendors']]
    print(f"  Ring ({ring['hops']} hops): {' ↔ '.join(vendor_names)}")

The query catches the circular invoicing ring with 100% recall.

Pattern 3: How to Detect Money Mule Networks

In a money mule setup, multiple shell entities funnel money into a single account controlled by a syndicate. The individual disbursements are small, but the fan-in degree of the destination account is anomalously high.

You can uncover this pattern by performing degree analysis on destination bank accounts:

// graph/queries.py — detect_money_mule_rings()
MATCH (a:BankAccount)<-[p_paid:PAID_TO]-(p:Payment)-[:LINKED_TO]->(i:Invoice)
                  -[:ISSUED_BY]->(v:Vendor)
WITH a, collect(DISTINCT v) AS vendors,
     sum(p.amount) AS total_received,
     count(DISTINCT v) AS unique_vendors,
     count(p) AS payment_count
WHERE unique_vendors >= $min_vendors
RETURN a.account_id,
       a.routing_number,
       a.bank_name,
       unique_vendors AS vendor_count,
       payment_count,
       total_received AS total_amount,
       [vendor IN vendors | vendor.name] AS vendor_names
ORDER BY unique_vendors DESC

You can use the following risk guide to evaluate accounts based on incoming connections:

Vendor CountRisk Level
1–3Normal
4–9Investigate
10+Likely money mule

In production, you can add a threshold on total received amount to minimize false positives:

WHERE unique_vendors >= 10 AND total_received > 50000

Running the detection query in Python:

mules = queries.detect_money_mule_rings(min_vendor_count=5)
for acct in mules:
    print(f"  {acct['a.account_id']} ({acct['a.bank_name']}) | "
          f"{acct['vendor_count']} vendors | ${acct['total_amount']:.0f}")

The query successfully identifies the injected mule ring (ACC-MULE-001), which aggregates payments across 25 shell vendors.

Pattern 4: How to Identify Vendor Collusion Clusters

Colluding shell companies often mask their affiliation by registering under different corporate names. But they frequently leak metadata, such as shared physical office suites or identical banking branch routing prefixes.

To identify these clusters, you can evaluate multiple derived relationships concurrently and compute a composite structural risk score:

// graph/queries.py — detect_vendor_collusion()
MATCH (v:Vendor)
OPTIONAL MATCH (v)-[:SHARED_ACCOUNT_WITH]->(v2)
OPTIONAL MATCH (v)-[:SHARED_LOCATION]->(v3)
OPTIONAL MATCH (v)-[:SHARED_ROUTING_PREFIX]->(v4)
WITH v,
     collect(DISTINCT v2) AS shared_account_vendors,
     collect(DISTINCT v3) AS shared_location_vendors,
     collect(DISTINCT v4) AS shared_routing_vendors
WITH v,
     size(shared_account_vendors) AS sc,
     size(shared_location_vendors) AS sl,
     size(shared_routing_vendors) AS sr
WHERE (sc + sl + sr) >= $min_score AND (sc + sl + sr) > 0
RETURN v.name AS vendor,
       v.tax_id,
       (sc + sl + sr) AS risk_score,
       [n IN shared_account_vendors + shared_location_vendors + shared_routing_vendors | n.name] AS related_vendors,
       [x IN range(1, sc) | 'shared_account'] +
       [x IN range(1, sl) | 'shared_location'] +
       [x IN range(1, sr) | 'shared_routing'] AS flags
ORDER BY risk_score DESC

Key points here:

  • Using OPTIONAL MATCH is essential here. A strict MATCH would drop vendors that exhibit shared routing and location but haven't yet shared a bank account.
  • You can tune the risk score based on your business environment. Sharing a city is common in large commercial hubs, but sharing a routing prefix and an office suite at the same time elevates the composite score past the investigative threshold.
collusion = queries.detect_vendor_collusion(min_risk_score=2)
for vendor in collusion[:10]:
    print(f"  {vendor['vendor']} | Risk: {vendor['risk_score']} | "
          f"Flags: {vendor['flags']}")

The multi-attribute scoring query successfully flags the four-vendor collusion cluster.

Pattern 5: How to Flag Out-of-Jurisdiction Payment Approvals

Internal fraud often relies on an employee approving an invoice outside their departmental authority. For instance, an HR manager might approve an engineering infrastructure vendor invoice without authorization.

Approval systems often confirm that an approver has signing authority, but they rarely validate whether the approver's department has jurisdiction over the invoice category. A graph query can traverse the full approval path and evaluate departmental permissions:

// graph/queries.py — detect_payment_anomalies()
MATCH (inv:Invoice)<-[:LINKED_TO]-(p:Payment),
      (e:Employee)-[:APPROVED]->(p),
      (e)-[:WORKS_FOR]->(org:Organization)
WITH inv, p, e, org,
     CASE
       WHEN inv.category = 'procurement' AND
            e.department IN ['finance', 'operations', 'procurement']
            THEN 'ok'
       WHEN inv.category = 'payroll' AND
            e.department IN ['hr', 'finance']
            THEN 'ok'
       WHEN inv.category = 'travel' AND
            e.department IN ['operations', 'finance', 'hr']
            THEN 'ok'
       WHEN inv.category = 'marketing' AND
            e.department IN ['marketing', 'finance']
            THEN 'ok'
       WHEN inv.category = 'consulting' AND
            e.department IN ['finance', 'operations', 'procurement']
            THEN 'ok'
       WHEN inv.category = 'services' AND
            e.department IN ['finance', 'operations', 'procurement']
            THEN 'ok'
       WHEN inv.category = 'supplies' AND
            e.department IN ['operations', 'procurement', 'finance']
            THEN 'ok'
       WHEN inv.category = 'maintenance' AND
            e.department IN ['operations', 'procurement', 'finance']
            THEN 'ok'
       WHEN inv.category = 'software' AND
            e.department IN ['engineering', 'operations', 'finance']
            THEN 'ok'
       ELSE 'ANOMALY'
     END AS approval_status
WHERE approval_status = 'ANOMALY'
RETURN inv.invoice_id, inv.amount, inv.category,
       inv.vendor_name, inv.date,
       e.name AS approver, e.employee_id,
       e.department AS approver_department
ORDER BY inv.date DESC

Key points here:

  • The default-deny 
    ELSE 'ANOMALY'
    structure ensures that any invoice category not explicitly authorized fails closed.
  • In enterprise architectures, you should materialize this policy logic directly in the graph using 
    (:Department)-[:AUTHORIZED_FOR]->(:Category)
    nodes rather than hardcoding values in queries. This allows compliance teams to update authority matrices without deploying new code.
anomalies = queries.detect_payment_anomalies()
print(f"Found {len(anomalies)} anomalous approvals")
for a in anomalies:
    print(f"  Invoice {a['inv.invoice_id']}: "
          f"{a['e.name']} ({a['e.department']}) approved "
          f"{a['inv.category']} | ${a['inv.amount']}")

The query surfaces all 3 injected approval anomalies with 100% recall.

How to Run the End-to-End Pipeline and Validate Results

You can orchestrate these steps into an automated command-line pipeline:

python analysis/run_detections.py

The end-to-end data flow operates in six distinct phases:

Generate Dataset → Load to Neo4j → Build Derived Relationships → Run 5 Queries → Save Results → Validate

How to Run Ingestion and Detection

The main pipeline script orchestrates data generation, schema creation, relationship materialization, and query execution:

# analysis/run_detections.py
from dataset.generate import FraudDatasetGenerator
from graph.connection import FraudGraph
from graph.loader import FraudGraphLoader
from graph.queries import FraudQueries

def run_pipeline(output_dir='analysis/output', force_regenerate=False):
    os.makedirs(output_dir, exist_ok=True)

    # Step 1: Generate or load dataset
    dataset_path = os.path.join(output_dir, 'data')
    if not os.path.exists(os.path.join(dataset_path, 'vendors.json')) or force_regenerate:
        gen = FraudDatasetGenerator(seed=42)
        gen.save(dataset_path)
    else:
        print(f'Dataset already at: {dataset_path}')

    # Load JSON files
    data = {}
    for name in ['vendors', 'invoices', 'payments', 'bank_accounts',
                  'employees', 'organizations', 'ground_truth']:
        with open(os.path.join(dataset_path, f'{name}.json')) as f:
            data[name] = json.load(f)

    # Step 2: Load into Neo4j
    graph = FraudGraph()
    graph.connect()
    graph.create_constraints()
    loader = FraudGraphLoader(graph)
    loader.load_all(data)
    loader.create_shared_account_relationships()
    loader.create_attribute_based_relationships()

    info = graph.get_info()
    print('Graph loaded:')
    for label, count in sorted(info['nodes'].items(), key=lambda x: -x[1]):
        print(f'  {label}: {count} nodes')

    # Step 3: Run all detections
    queries = FraudQueries(graph)
    results = queries.detect_all()

    # Step 4: Save results
    with open(os.path.join(output_dir, 'detection_results.json'), 'w') as f:
        json.dump(results, f, indent=2, default=str)

    for pattern, items in results.items():
        print(f'  {pattern}: {len(items)} findings')

The 

detect_all()
method runs all five queries and returns a single dict:
# graph/queries.py
def detect_all(self):
    return {
        'duplicate_invoices': self.detect_duplicates(),
        'circular_schemes': self.detect_circular_schemes(),
        'money_mule_rings': self.detect_money_mule_rings(),
        'vendor_collusion': self.detect_vendor_collusion(),
        'payment_anomalies': self.detect_payment_anomalies(),
    }

How to Validate Recall Against Injected Ground Truth

The validation script compares query results against the ground-truth file to measure recall:

# analysis/validate.py
from collections import defaultdict

def validate(results_path, output_path=None):
    with open(results_path) as f:
        results = json.load(f)

    with open(os.path.join(os.path.dirname(results_path), 'data',
                           'ground_truth.json')) as f:
        ground_truth = json.load(f)

    gt_by_pattern = defaultdict(list)
    for pattern in ground_truth:
        gt_by_pattern[pattern['pattern']].append(pattern)

The verification logic evaluates detection accuracy for each pattern type:

for pattern_name, gt_patterns in gt_by_pattern.items():
    found = results.get(pattern_name, [])
    gt_count = len(gt_patterns)

    if pattern_name == 'duplicate_invoices':
        print(f"DUPLICATE INVOICES: DETECTED {len(found)} of {gt_count} pairs — {len(found)/max(1,gt_count):.0%} recall")

    elif pattern_name == 'money_mule_rings':
        matched = sum(1 for gt in gt_patterns
                      for r in found
                      if r.get('a.account_id') == gt['shared_account'])
        print(f"MONEY MULE RINGS: DETECTED {matched} of {gt_count} rings — {matched/max(1,gt_count):.0%} recall")

Running the validator against a dataset generated with 

seed=42
produces these results:
DUPLICATE INVOICES: DETECTED 12 of 12 pairs — 100% recall
CIRCULAR SCHEMES: DETECTED 1 of 1 rings — 100% recall
MONEY MULE RINGS: DETECTED 1 of 1 rings — 100% recall
VENDOR COLLUSION: 89 high-risk vendors flagged (multi-attribute scoring)
PAYMENT ANOMALIES: DETECTED 3 of 3 anomalies — 100% recall

How to Execute the Complete Workflow

Here's the complete sequence of terminal commands to set up the environment, run the pipeline, and validate the results:

# 1. Start Neo4j
docker compose up -d

# 2. Install dependencies
pip install -r requirements.txt

# 3. Run the full pipeline
python analysis/run_detections.py

# 4. Validate results
python analysis/validate.py

# 5. (Optional) Regenerate with fresh data and re-run
python analysis/run_detections.py --regenerate

Production Architecture: How to Scale the Graph Pipeline

While the reference prototype operates on hundreds of nodes, production fraud detection engines handle millions of transactions daily. Scaling this architecture requires addressing key operational bottlenecks.

New Transaction
    ↓
Stage 1 — Deterministic queries (fast, rule-based)
    ↓  (if any pattern matches)
Stage 2 — ML scoring on graph features
    ↓
Risk Score → Alert / Approve / Escalate

How to Implement a Two-Stage Detection Architecture

Running global cycle detection queries synchronously on every incoming transaction inside an online payment path will exhaust database connection pools.

Instead, you should partition detection into two tiers:

  • Stage 1 (Synchronous Gating): Sub-millisecond Cypher queries that catch known patterns. They're fast because they use indexed properties, pre-built relationships, and bounded pattern lengths.
  • Stage 2 (Asynchronous Graph Analytics): For transactions that don't trigger a deterministic rule, compute graph-derived features and score them:

How to Tune Thresholds and Manage False Positives

Detection systems inevitably produce false positives. In production, review feedback from compliance analysts should be used to continuously calibrate query thresholds:

#Tune thresholds based on false positive rate

queries.detect_money_mule_rings(min_vendor_count=10) # was 5
queries.detect_duplicates(max_days_apart=7) # was 14
queries.detect_vendor_collusion(min_risk_score=3) # was 2

You can rerun validation after each threshold update to monitor the effect on recall:

python analysis/validate.py --input analysis/output/detection_results.json

How to Mitigate Supernode Expansion

A common failure in graph systems is the "supernode" problem. Legitimate shared entities (for example, a major corporate landlord, a national power utility, or internal payroll accounts) can accumulate tens of thousands of incoming edges.

When a query attempts to traverse through a supernode without filtering, traversal latency spikes exponentially.

You can mitigate this with two strategies:

  • Degree Limits: Add degree pruning in traversals:

MATCH (a:BankAccount)

WHERE size((a)<-[:PAID_TO]-()) < 1000

  • Node Labels: Tag known high-volume institutional entities with a :Whitelisted or :Utility label, and explicitly exclude them from collusion and money mule scans.

How to Use Graph Features for Machine Learning

The most effective fraud detection systems don't treat graphs and machine learning as competing paradigms. Instead, the graph acts as an advanced feature store for predictive models:

  • Degree Centrality: Measures the connectivity of an account to identify mule convergence.
  • Betweenness Centrality: Identifies entities that act as bridges between seemingly disconnected vendor groups.
  • PageRank and Community Detection: Quantifies cluster association and entity importance across the network.

An ML classifier relying solely on transaction amounts might see nothing unusual about a $4,900 payment. But when paired with a graph-derived feature showing the vendor has a high betweenness centrality and shares a second-degree connection with a confirmed fraud ring, the classifier flags the transaction with high precision.

Key Architectural Lessons and Takeaways

Building and tuning graph-based fraud pipelines highlights several key trade-offs:

First, in a relational database, schema design prioritizes third normal form (3NF) to eliminate data redundancy. In a graph, design your schema around the traversals you need to execute. If a query repeatedly traverses four hops to find correlated attributes, materialize that correlation as a direct relationship during ingestion.

Second, unique property constraints aren't just for data integrity. They provide the underlying hash indexes that make node lookups $O(1)$. Omitting constraints turns every graph merge into an unindexed full scan.

Third, you should curate the rule Inventory**.** Start with a focused set of four or five high-signal patterns. Each pattern requires threshold calibration and triage workflows. Adding dozens of unverified heuristics simultaneously creates operational noise and alert fatigue for compliance teams.

And finally, close the analyst feedback loop. The output of a detection query is a hypothesis, not a final verdict. When compliance analysts investigate an alert and confirm fraud, write that status back into the graph as a node property or label (for example, :ConfirmedFraud). This enriches the neighborhood topology and provides clean ground truth for training downstream machine learning models.

Conclusion

In this tutorial, you explored why point-in-time relational checks miss complex fraud schemes, how to model accounts payable data as an interconnected graph, and how to materialize derived edges to accelerate traversal latency.

You also implemented five Cypher queries capable of detecting duplicate billing, circular rings, money mules, vendor collusion, and unauthorized payment approvals.

The companion code for this article is available at github.com/kamalct/fraud-detection-knowledge-graphs. All data is synthetic and fully reproducible.

entries.title: How AI-Powered Search Works: A Guide for Devs on AI Visibility
entries.summary: Searched worked in a familiar way for decades: you'd type in your query, get back a list of pages, and choose one to click on. Behind the scenes, Google would find the pages it thought you might want,
entries.content:
Searched worked in a familiar way for decades: you'd type in your query, get back a list of pages, and choose one to click on. Behind the scenes, Google would find the pages it thought you might want, rank them, and give you a list of options.

But AI-powered search is changing that experience. If you ask ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity, or another AI system a question, you may not get a long list of links to check out. Instead, the system can interpret your question, gather information from different sources when applicable, and generate an answer directly.

This changes something important for websites and brands: what happens when there's no traditional ranking position to fight for?

This is where the idea of AI visibility comes in. Instead of asking only, "Where does my website rank?", businesses and publishers are increasingly asking a different question: "Does the AI mention us when someone asks a relevant question?"

That distinction may sound small, but it represents a major change in how information is discovered online. And it's what we'll explore here.

What We'll Cover:

Google Gives You Ranked Results, While AI Gives You an Answer

If you're trying to understand how a search engine and an answer engine really work, it comes down to how each handles information retrieval.

Traditional search engines crawl the web, catalog pages in an index, run ranking algorithms against a user's keywords, and display candidate URLs ordered by perceived authority and link equity. The final decision of what to actually click on and read remains entirely in the hands of the person asking the question.

AI search changes things up a bit. When a user enters a natural-language prompt, the AI model decomposes the underlying intent, identifies candidate information using Retrieval-Augmented Generation (an AI technique that improves the accuracy of LLM models) or its pre-trained parametric memory, reconciles conflicting viewpoints, and actively decides which resources or solutions to present.

The most critical takeaway is that ranking highly on Google doesn't guarantee an AI engine will mention you. In fact, an Ahrefs citation study analyzing thousands of prompts discovered that only about 12% of URLs cited by generative assistants like ChatGPT and Copilot actually ranked in Google's top 10 for the exact query.

While Google’s own AI Overviews pull more frequently from conventional search results, standalone conversational engines construct independent answer graphs. AI visibility doesn't really care about claiming a specific URL slot. What matters more is whether your brand (and its resources) shows up as part of the machine’s direct answer.

What Does “AI Visibility” Actually Mean?

If you strip away all the marketing language, AI visibility represents the probability and quality of your brand’s inclusion inside a synthesized response. Evaluating it requires breaking down three distinct dimensions:

  • Brand mentions: The model explicitly names your company, service, or product within the prose of its answer. For example, if someone asks for lightweight running shoes, does your shoe article make the bulleted recommendation list?
  • Citations: The model footnotes or links back to your specific web page as an authoritative source for the information it just presented.
  • Context and sentiment: The way in which the model portrays the brand. Being mentioned as a budget-friendly option differs significantly from being characterized as unreliable or out of date.

This distinction matters because mentions and citations don't always happen together. An AI model can freely recommend your product because it understands your brand as a recognized entity, but cite a third-party tech review site as its primary factual reference. On the other hand, an engine might cite your documentation to clarify an API standard without ever suggesting your company as a vendor.

So How Does an AI Decide What to Show?

In order to appreciate how the AI chooses entities to include in its search results, we need to explore how modern retrieval engines work.

Current systems don't use only matching algorithms. They also incorporate elements of semantic analysis (the process by which an AI or computer program interprets the real meaning and context of words), vector representations (a way of turning words, sentences, or data into lists of numbers so that computers can understand their meaning) and multi-source verification (the practice of cross-checking a claim or dataset across multiple independent and reliable origins to confirm its truth and accuracy).

After the user provides the prompt, the system doesn't treat it as a set of words to be matched with an index. Using dense passage retrieval and Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), the engine translates the request into a high-dimensional vector embedding of the real semantic context. The system then searches candidate passages on the internet, analyzing them through a variety of signals:

Core Signal

What the Engine Evaluates

Why It Impacts the Response

Semantic Relevance

Meaning, context, and vector proximity

Resolves the user's underlying intent rather than verbatim text.

Information Density

Presence of hard data, statistics, and verifiable claims

Models favor text rich in concrete facts over vague qualitative descriptions.

Attribution & Provenance

Citations and attributed external references

Transparent sourcing allows the model to ground its claims safely.

Cross-Source Consensus

Corroboration across independent platforms

If independent review boards concur, models accept facts as the truth.

Information Freshness

Recent timestamps and active updates

Ensures specs, pricing, and availability reflect current market realities.

Structural Extractability

Clean semantic hierarchy (HTML tags, tables)

Modular, clean blocks allow the model to lift passages without misinterpretation.

The mathematical backing supporting these signals was found in the groundbreaking Princeton University GEO study. Through experimentation with 10,000 queries on various generative search engines, the scientists confirmed that tailored content changes may increase visibility of the source in AI results by 30% to 40%.

More importantly, the study revealed the hierarchy of what kind of rewards a generative model can give:

  • Addition of statistics: The inclusion of quantitative information resulted in an increase in visibility by 41%. AI algorithms prefer quantifiable statistics rather than generalizations such as "many users prefer..." or "highly efficient...".
  • Addition of quotation/citation: Citing subject matter experts in the form of quotes and providing sources resulted in a 28% to 40% increase in visibility.
  • Traditional keyword stuffing as a penalty: Traditional SEO relied heavily on repetition of keywords for optimization purposes. But the Princeton study showed that keyword stuffing lowered visibility by 10% below the baseline in models such as Perplexity because LLMs recognize repetition as manipulative text.

Also, studies done on retrieval-augmented LLM search in the International Journal of Information Management Data Insights show that conversational engines have very strict checks for neutrality and consistency before showing a brand. If the claims made by the website cannot be proven through consensus from third parties like respected industry databases, academic databases or peer discussions, the engine filters out that entity from its database to reduce risks of hallucinations.

The kind of query determines the whole selection process. For example, an uncomplicated query like "what is GPS?" will call for an encyclopedic response from educational repositories. On the other hand, an operational query like "what is the best running watch for marathon training" calls for comparative retrieval. In this case, the model crosschecks things like battery power, GPS reviews from running communities and opinions from enthusiasts.

The AI doesn't choose the website with the most backlinks, or other seemingly predictable features. Instead, it chooses websites that satisfy the different aspects of the user's context with verifiable evidence.

The Strange Thing About AI Search: Smaller Sites Can Still Win

In traditional SEO, established monoliths with vast numbers of backlinks often have unshakable monopolies on high-volume searches. AI search, on the other hand, works on a completely different principle: it favors utility rather than sheer domain dominance.

Since AI search engines seek answers to particular aspects of the request, specialist publishers, small agencies, and producers of niche products tend to outrank major brands. A 2,000-word article on how to debug an edge-case problem of a particular software created by one developer carries much more value for the synthesis engine than the standard 3,000-word blog post written by a corporation and padded with introductory phrases.

The data shows that mentions of a brand online are highly correlated with generative citations but not legacy backlink volume. The analysis of 680 million AI citations showed that the cited sources of one engine could vastly differ from the sources of another engine. Even ChatGPT and Perplexity shared just 11% of citations due to the uniqueness of retrieval models.

How Do You Measure Something That Doesn’t Have a Ranking?

In the context of answers being dynamically combined within conversation threads, the conventional ranking tracker becomes far less valuable. There's no set "position four" in a dynamic chat system. Two distinct users who enter identical prompts might receive custom-made responses from entirely separate source materials.

To solve this problem, the industry has started moving toward new metrics for evaluation. A clear sign that this is happening is through the use of AI leaderboards to track the frequency with which certain brands show up in conversational answer engines.

These tools gauge generative share of voice through simulation of the queries made in real life in categories, countries, and engines. Rather than tracking the ranking of the keyword in a static manner, the teams analyze the prompts that lead to mentions and the primary websites mentioned for factual support.

What the Data Tells Us About AI Search

When we analyze the aggregated data regarding AI visibility, we can identify a few key patterns in terms of citations that are generated by the models.

First, independently developed aggregators and review websites have higher citation value compared to sites owned by brands themselves. When answering comparison questions regarding products, the generative model tends to avoid creating an impression of a biased promotional message. Citing the vendor's website to explain why it's the best choice is against the principle of neutrality. That's why editorial publications, testing labs, and online forums such as Reddit or Quora are chosen as primary sources while the brand's domain is cited incidentally.

Secondly, the engine's architecture sets citation practices. The following deep analysis benchmark shows that various engines give citations to quite different areas of the internet:

  • ChatGPT refers mostly to encyclopedia sources, news publishers, and wide-ranging reference sources.
  • Perplexity gives preference to forum threads, developers' sites, and live discussions.
  • Google AI Overviews rely mainly on the current top search index and use excerpts directly from reliable commercial sites.

For instance, when considering a highly competitive market such as cloud storage, one cloud may stand out in suggestions not because of increased advertising, but because of how much their documentation is searched in various forums, such as Reddit and Stack Overflow.

What This Means for Developers and Content Creators

Adapting to an AI-mediated web requires re-evaluating how pages are built, structured, and maintained. For developers, technical writers, and content creators, the focus moves from keyword targeting to machine legibility.

Structure for Extraction

Generative engines break down long-form text into smaller chunks called embeddings. If a page uses convoluted layouts where answers are buried beneath promotional intros or client-side JavaScript, crawlers may fail to extract the core information.

  • Use descriptive
    and
    tags that mirror explicit questions.
  • Place direct, unambiguous answers in the first sentence beneath each heading.
  • Use native HTML tables and clean bulleted lists for comparative specs rather than custom canvas widgets.

Provide Verifiable Fact Anchors

LLMs are trained to prioritize consensus and avoid unsupported claims. You can make your material easier for systems to validate by anchoring observations to real data points:

  • Include clear author credentials, primary research data, and direct source links.
  • Keep factual documentation (like pricing tiers, integration methods, and release numbers) regularly updated. Outdated content gets discarded during retrieval filtering.
  • Adopt standard schema markup (
    Article
    , 
    TechArticle
    , 
    Product
    , 
    FAQPage
    ) to give automated scrapers unambiguous metadata.

Optimize for Questions, Not Query Fragments

Traditional search encouraged queries like "best lightweight laptop battery life." In contrast, users converse with AI using conversational questions: "Which 14-inch laptop can last through an 8-hour flight while running Docker containers?" Creating content that tackles specific, multi-layered scenarios ensures your page contains the exact semantic nodes an AI needs to construct a complete recommendation.

SEO Isn't Dead. The Metric Is Just Changing.

The arrival of generative search has sparked familiar predictions about the death of search engine optimization. But SEO isn't disappearing. It's splitting into two complementary disciplines:

  • Traditional search engines remain critical drivers of internet traffic
  • AI engines still rely on the open web's index to replenish their knowledge bases

A healthy site architecture, fast page load speeds, and credible editorial standards remain prerequisites for both models.

What has changed is the definition of success. A website can hold a top organic rank on a conventional search page and remain absent from an AI’s spoken summary. Conversely, a focused technical guide can fuel an AI's answers across millions of chat prompts without ever ranking on page one for a head keyword.

Google taught us how to fight for that top spot on the results page. But AI search challenges us to become the trusted source material that models rely on when they synthesize knoweldge for their users.

The creators and brands that win in this next era won't be those who game the algorithm for clicks, but those who publish the clearest, most authoritative, and most easily verified answers on the web.

Wrapping Up

The biggest change in search doesn't have to do with AI replacing Google. The most significant change is actually that AI is changing what it means to be visible online.

A high ranking can still bring traffic, but ranking is no longer the only thing that matters. As more people ask AI systems for direct answers, brands and websites also need to think about whether their information is actually being selected, cited, and included in those answers.

In the end, the goal is pretty simple: create information that genuinely answers questions, is easy to access, and is trustworthy enough to be used. Because in AI search, you want your site to be part of the answer.

entries.content:
Understanding how malicious actors infiltrate networks is the first step to building resilient infrastructure.

To help developers and aspiring security analysts learn the fundamentals of offensive security legally and safely, we just released How Ethical Hackers Actually Break Into Systems on the freeCodeCamp.org YouTube channel.

Taught by cybersecurity instructor Declan Middleton, this 2.5 hour crash course walks through terminal navigation, target reconnaissance, vulnerability assessment, web exploitation, and automation scripting against a dedicated Capture The Flag (CTF) virtual machine.

Core Skills Covered

  • Linux and Terminal Operations

    Master command line navigation, permission modeling, user management, and process execution inside Parrot OS.
  • Network Reconnaissance with Nmap

    Scan target IPs to identify active hosts, open ports, running services, and specific software versions using stealth and decoy flags.
  • Web Content Discovery and Fuzzing

    Enumerate hidden directories, files, and endpoints using tools such as Dirsearch, FFuF, WhatWeb, and Nikto.
  • Request Analysis and Exploitation with Burp Suite

    Intercept, inspect, and modify HTTP requests to audit authentication workflows and execute file upload attacks with webshells.
  • Automated Security Tooling in Bash and Python

    Write custom reconnaissance scripts to automate socket connections, banner grabbing, and HTTP header parsing without manual overhead.

Watch the full tutorial on the freeCodeCamp.org YouTube channel to set up your isolated lab and practice ethical hacking techniques from scratch (3-hour watch).

entries.title: High-Speed Decision Pipelines: Jev and Prefill-Only Inference from Scratch
entries.summary: Autoregressive token generation is notoriously slow and memory-intensive, especially when you only need a model to make a structured classification or routing decision rather than write out paragraphs
entries.content:
Autoregressive token generation is notoriously slow and memory-intensive, especially when you only need a model to make a structured classification or routing decision rather than write out paragraphs of text.

To help engineers bypass autoregressive bottlenecks, freeCodeCamp just released the Jev Course: Prefill-Only Inference and Decision Models from Scratch.

This in-depth PyTorch guide walks you through building blazing-fast, decision-oriented architectures that process inputs entirely within the initial prefill stage.

What You Will Learn

  • Prefill-Only Architecture

    Learn how to eliminate token-by-token decoding loops to run ultra-low latency classifications and actions directly from prompt evaluation.
  • Encoder and Decoder Design

    Build both model variants from scratch in PyTorch to understand the mathematical trade-offs between bidirectional representations and causal flows.
  • Custom Causal Masking

    Implement low-level attention masks that preserve directional dependencies without introducing unnecessary padding overhead.
  • KV-Cache Reuse Strategies

    Harness key-value cache states across continuous decision pipelines to process repetitive system contexts with minimal redundant compute.

You can watch the full Jev Course: Prefill-Only Inference and Decision Models from Scratch video on YouTube to start optimizing your custom language model inference workflows (2-hour watch).
